newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FULL TEXT-RBA's Fraser comments to parliamentary committee.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FULL TEXT-RBA's Fraser comments to parliamentary committee.

text.p: The following is full text of Reserve Bank of Australia governor Bernie Fraser's opening remarks to the House of Representativesa Standing Committee on Financial Institutions and Public Administration:
Mr Chairman, this is the Reserve Bank's fifth annual appearance before this Committee, but the first time under your Chairmanship.
I would like to begin, therefore, by reiterating that we welcome these meetings with the Committee and, as in the past, we will do what we can to make them informative and constructive.
Despite occasional assertions to the contrary, the Reserve Bank is and has been a very independent central bank.

And we take very seriously the responsibilities which go with that independence, including the responsibility to explain carefully to the public, to Parliament and to others what we are doing and why - in the jargon, to be transparent and accountable.
One - but by no means the only - vehicle for this purpose is the Bank s Annual Report, the latest version of which is the focus of our meeting today.
The content of this document has increased by about 50 per cent over the past seven years.
In that time there has been a substantial increase in the flow of information from the Bank in articles in its monthly Bulletin, in speeches by senior officers of the Bank, and in other ways.
Any serious student of the Reserve Bank and its operations has access to a good deal more information today than ever before.

I mention these developments because, with so much information now in the public arena, it is hard to say much that is new in an opening statement like this, or to know the angles which might be of particular interest to the Committee.
I will, therefore, confine these opening remarks to a few of the general matters covered in the Annual Report and, with my colleagues, endeavour to answer your particular questions.
THE ECONOMY AND MONETARY POLICY
As usual, performance across different sectors is varied but, overall, the economy continues to grow at a relatively robust rate, with low inflation.
Total GDP grew by 4 per cent over the course of 1995/96, and non-farm GDP grew by 3.75 percent.
We have now had five years of non-inflationary growth since the recovery commenced in mid-1991, with GDP averaging a little over 3.50 per cent a year, and inflation averaging 2.50 per cent.
This combination puts Australia among the very top performers among OECD countries over this period.
The budget time forecasts for 1996/97 envisage a sixth year of growth of around 3.50 per cent, with inflation of about 2.75 per cent.
We agree generally with these forecasts, but we think inflation through 1996/97 could turn out to be a little lower.

The growth forecasts are underpinned by a reasonably encouraging outlook for our major trading partners, good levels of business and consumer confidence, and the absence of any major "imbalances" in the domestic economy.

The further large rise expected in business investment - up 14 per cent in 1996/97 - is an important key to achieving the growth forecast. Consumer and government spending are both forecast to grow by about 3 per cent.
At 3.1 per cent, underlying inflation in the year to the June quarter was a little above the 2-3 per cent average the Bank is aiming for over the course of the business cycle.

We are as confident as we can ever be in economic forecasting that when the figure for the year to the September quarter is released next month it will be comfortably within the 2-3 per cent band - and that it will remain there over the year ahead.
The headline rate is likely to come back even more sharply.
Hopefully, this new environment of relative price stability will be reflected in new wage bargains.
The inflation target, expressed in the way it is, is helpful to the Bank in pursuing its monetary policy objectives; I
think it is also helpful in bringing an element of predictability to the pervasive uncertainty that is always present in the economy at large, and in the financial markets in particular.

The Bank does not have an explicit target for employment or unemployment, but we do pay particular attention to trends in these areas. We do so because our "charter" requires us to but, more importantly, because it is sensible to do so.
The best contribution the Bank can make to reducing unemployment is to do what it can to sustain a good rate of economic growth.

This involves the Bank in making judgments about future developments in the economy and adjusting monetary policy in a forward looking (or pre-emptive) way - in both directions. There were elements of this in the 15 rate reductions made between January 1990 and July 1993 - which contributed to the economic recovery - and in the three rate increases in the second half of 1994 - which helped to return growth to a sustainable rate when it threatened to accelerate too rapidly.
Unemployment declined from a peak of over 11 per cent at the end of 1992 to 8.5 per cent in the middle of 1995.
It has been stuck around that level over the past year.

This stalling in the unemployment rate, together with the expected fall in inflation, prompted the Bank to reduce the overnight cash rate - the interest rate which the Bank controls - by half a percentage point (to 7 per cent) at the end of July;

the full effects of the flow-ons of that rate reduction to interest rates charged by banks and other financial institutions will only become apparent in the economic indicators to be released over the months ahead.
Despite the relatively strong growth forecast for 1996/97, the unemployment rate is forecast to decline only marginally over the year ahead - and to remain around 8.25 per cent in mid-1997.
While the budget forecasts can be viewed as the mid-points in a range of probable outcomes, they are subject to significant margins of error - in both directions.

The Reserve Bank is alert to these risks and will be monitoring developments closely; as always, it will be paying particular attention to the indicators bearing upon trends in inflation and in unemployment.
FINANCIAL MARKET DEVELOPMENTS
Financial markets continue to be influenced by both international and domestic developments.
The increasing globalisation of financial markets means that movements in bond yields and share prices in Australia tend to show a strong correlation with overseas - and especially U.S. - movements.
These closer linkages between capital markets are supplementing the traditional role played by the exchange rate in transmitting international influences to Australia.

Such international linkages do not diminish the Bank s control over monetary policy - which continues to be determined primarily on developments in the domestic economy - but policy makers need to be mindful of them.

The improvement in Australia s inflation performance and prospects over recent years has seen a marked narrowing of the differentials between Australian and overseas long-term interest rates; these are the rates which are determined primarily in
the market place, and not by policy makers.
The differential between yields on Australian and US 10-year bonds, for example, has narrowed from 300 points five years ago to 250 points one year ago to 120 points now.
New Zealand, which has had significantly higher short-term interest rates than Australia over the past four years, also has higher long-term interest rates than Australia now.
This reduction in the inflation premium built into Australia's interest rates is benefiting both private and government borrowers.
The exchange rate of the Australian dollar has rebounded from the unusually low levels of a year ago, mainly in response to improved prospects for the world economy and commodity prices.
In Trade Weighted Index (TWI) terms, the rise in the Australian dollar over the past year was about 9 per cent.
A more relevant comparison is with the average level of the past 10 years when the TWI fluctuated around a flat trend; on that basis, today s TWI is 4 per cent above that average level.

Given that recent movements in the exchange rate have been well based (ie they have tended to reflect "fundamental" rather than speculative factors), the Bank has not intervened in the market to influence the exchange rate.

As noted in the Annual Report, however, the Bank has made substantial purchases of foreign exchange during the past year, both to cover the Government's needs for foreign exchange, and, on its own account, to facilitate a further run-off of outstanding swaps accumulated during 1992 and 1993 when the Bank had intervened heavily to support the Australian dollar.
At the margin, these purchases probably have held back the appreciation of the Australian dollar a little.
BANKING AND THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM
The past year has seen increased competition in banking, and not only in wholesale banking, which has always been very competitive, but also in the retail market.

Largely because of the increased competition from mortgage originators, mortgage interest rates have fallen even though official rates remained unchanged - and they have fallen for all borrowers, not only for new borrowers.
This competition in housing in particular can be expected to hasten the decline in banks interest margins, but we will have to await more data to see this; the latest available data
relate to the six months to the March quarter of 1996.
In the meanwhile, most banks reported increased profits in 1995/96.

Other measures also indicate that the industry overall is quite healthy, with bad loans equivalent to only 1 per cent of total assets, compared with the peak of 6 per cent in early 1992. The average capital ratio for all banks is currently a
little over 11 per cent, comfortably above the minimum BIS requirement of 8 per cent.
Bank supervision is an evolutionary business, and a number of further changes were made during the past year in response to changing conditions and experiences.

These changes are documented in the Annual Report and include arrangements for incorporating market risks within the capital adequacy requirements; revised guidelines on the involvement of banks in funds management and securitisation activities; new arrangements for external auditors; and the
liberalisation of guidelines to permit banks to make equity investments.

The latest Annual Report also includes a special chapter on longer-term developments in the financial system, which contains some useful background information for people interested in the subject matter of the Wallis Inquiry.
This Committee has a copy of the Bank s submission to that Inquiry, and we can speak to its detail later if you wish.
For the moment, I would like to make two general comments:

(I) I think it is a very tall order to expect the Inquiry to come to grips with the complexities of the Australian financial system and advance recommendations for sensible improvements, in the short time available to it.

This task is not made any easier by the promotion of some quite radical proposals from certain stables, without much evident analysis of the perceived shortcomings of the present arrangements, or of the ramifications of the proposed arrangements.

The temptation to latch onto an overseas model of one sort or another and seek to transport it here, without fully appreciating how it operates in its home environment - let alone in a foreign environment - is quite scary.
(II) The bank accepts, of course, that there is always scope to improve present arrangements, and we have made some suggestions in our submission.

It is our belief, however, that guided evolutionary change is the way to go, and that to adopt radical proposals - such as a "mega regulator" or, at the other extreme, to rely entirely on "disclosure" - really would be flirting with disaster.
THE BANK'S OPERATIONS
The latest Annual Report also includes considerable information on the Bank's own operations during the past year.
I will not go into any detail here, but three points are worth mentioning:
(I) the Bank's net operating earnings for the year totalled almost $2.5 billion, compared with an average of $2.1 billion a year over the past decade;
(II) staff numbers declined marginally last year, after having fallen by half during the preceding decade; and
(III the Bank's operating costs declined further last year and, in real terms, are now about 20 per cent below their peak in 1991/92.
Mr Chairman, I think I have said more than enough to get the ball rolling. We are in your hands.
